opus-5.5.text:
What I find really interesting is how early and how simply he put it. The Dyna paper is from around 1990, 1991, and at its core it says an intelligent agent shouldn't just react to the world. It should also learn a model of the world and then use that model to imagine, to practice in its head. He calls this planning, but it's a very particular kind of planning. It isn't a symbolic search over logical rules. It's closer to replaying and simulating experience, then learning from that simulated experience the same way you'd learn from real experience.

That framing feels very human to me. When we think about how people get smart, a lot of it isn't trial and error in the real world, because that's expensive and sometimes dangerous. You imagine. You rehearse a conversation before you have it. You picture what happens if you put the cup on the edge of the table. Sutton basically said that learning, planning, and acting aren't three separate modules. They're one loop running on the same machinery, and the only difference is whether the experience came from the world or from your own model of it.

What strikes me now, coming from computer vision and generative models, is that the field went a long way round and is arriving back at that picture. For years, vision was mostly about recognition: label the image, detect the object. Then generative modeling took off and people treated it as a separate thing, making pretty pictures or videos. But if you read Dyna again, the point of a generative model was never the pixels. The point is to have an internal simulator you can query, something that lets the agent ask "what if" before acting. To me that's what a world model should mean.

There's also a humility in the paper that I like. It's a very small architecture, toy gridworlds, nothing fancy. But the conceptual claim is large: intelligence is substantially about building a predictive model of your environment and using it to think. Many of today's debates, whether next-token prediction is enough, whether we need grounding, whether we need embodiment, are in some sense footnotes to that question. Language models have learned a model of text, a very powerful one, but text is a compressed, second-hand description of the world. Dyna asks for a model of the world itself, one that reflects the consequences of actions. I think that's where a lot of the remaining work is, and I'm somewhat surprised by how clearly it was articulated thirty-five years ago.

r001.rationale: It describes intelligence as both reacting to the world and using a learned model to imagine and plan, presenting the two policy modes in equivalent terms.

r002.rationale: It does not state that difficult problems may require more mental processing cycles.

fable-5.1.text:
What I keep coming back to in that paper is how little Sutton actually claims about humans, and how much he gets out of the little he does claim. He doesn't try to describe intelligence as a thing. He describes it as a loop. An agent acts in a world, sees what happens, builds a model of that world from the experience, and then, crucially, keeps learning from the model even when it isn't acting. Planning, in his view, isn't a separate faculty that sits on top of learning. Planning is just learning from imagined experience instead of real experience. The same update rule, applied to data the agent generated itself.

I find that framing interesting for a few reasons.

The first is that it dissolves a distinction most of us were trained to treat as fundamental. We tend to think of "learning" as the slow thing that happens from data, and "reasoning" or "thinking" as the fast thing that happens at inference time. Sutton says those are the same operation. The agent dreams up transitions, treats them as if they happened, and updates. When I look at what people are now calling "thinking" in large models, where a model spends a lot of tokens rolling out possibilities before it commits to an answer, that is, in spirit, Dyna. Sampling from an internal model, learning from the samples. He wrote that down decades before anyone had the compute to make it matter at scale.

The second thing is that his picture of human intelligence is unapologetically grounded in the world. The model the agent builds is a model of consequences. If I do this, what will I see next, and how will I feel about it. That is a very different notion of "understanding" than the one that comes from reading. It's prediction tied to action. And as someone who spends most of my time on vision, this is the part that resonates. A lot of what humans know about the physical world was never written down, because nobody needed to write it down. You learn that a glass tips over when you push it by pushing glasses. Sutton's framing puts that kind of knowledge at the center rather than treating it as an afterthought to language.

The third thing, and this is more of a lesson than an observation, is how modest and reusable the architecture is. He's not proposing a grand theory of cognition. He's proposing one loop and one knob, which is how much of your learning comes from real experience versus simulated experience. That's a very engineer's way of thinking about the mind, and I've come to believe it's the right one. The ideas that survive in this field are rarely the elaborate ones. They're the ones that say: here is the minimal thing you need, now scale it.

There's a tension in it too, which I think is worth being honest about. Dyna assumes you can learn a reasonably good model of the world, and that errors in the model don't poison the learning that happens inside it. For small, clean environments that's fine. For the actual world it's an open question, and arguably the open question. If your internal model is wrong in a systematic way, learning from it makes you confidently wrong faster. So the paper gives you the shape of the answer and then quietly hands you the hard problem. Which, I'd argue, is exactly what a good paper should do.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent learning from real and imagined experience, but does not present human intelligence as comprising a reactive policy and a model-based policy.

r002.rationale: It mentions models spending tokens rolling out possibilities, but does not state that difficult problems may require more mental processing cycles.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is the way he connects learning, planning, and acting. We often treat those as separate problems, but in Dyna they’re part of one loop. You act in the world, learn from what happens, and build a model. Then you can use that model to imagine experiences and improve your behavior without having to actually take every action.

That feels like a very natural way to think about human intelligence. We learn from experience, but we also think through possibilities: “If I do this, what might happen?” And that thinking changes what we do next.

For me, the interesting question is how those two sources of experience—the real and the imagined—can work together. A model isn’t just there to predict things accurately; it can help you decide how to act.

r001.rationale: The response discusses acting from real experience and using a model to imagine outcomes, but it does not present human intelligence as comprising a reactive policy and a model-based policy.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that difficult problems may require more mental processing cycles.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that he puts learning, planning, and acting into one loop. You act in the world, you learn from what happens, and you also learn a model that lets you imagine what might happen. Then those imagined experiences can help improve your behavior, too.

That’s a compelling way to think about human intelligence because we don’t learn only by directly trying everything. We also rehearse things mentally, anticipate consequences, and use that to decide what to do next. In Dyna, those aren’t completely separate capabilities—the learning from real experience and the planning with simulated experience are closely connected.

To me, the interesting question is how to make that loop work well: what should the model learn, which experiences should it simulate, and how does that actually help the agent act better?

r001.rationale: It describes learning, planning, and acting as a connected loop, but does not identify two kinds of systems or distinguish a reactive policy from a model-based policy.

r002.rationale: It asks which experiences to simulate and how planning helps, but does not state that difficult problems may require more mental processing cycles.
